source.title: BitNet: Scaling 1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models
source.authors: Hongyu Wang; Shu-Ming Ma; Li Dong; Shao-Han Huang; Huai-Jie Wang; Ling-Xiao Ma; Fan Yang; Rui-Ping Wang; Yi Wu; Fu-Ru Wei

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model loss across model sizes and fits a power law, using the scaling-curve approach on BitNet and FP16 Transformers.
record.gate_note: The paper reports loss scaling with parameter count, a fit-based extrapolation for BitNet, downstream-task scaling, and loss against estimated inference energy. Quantization comparisons at a single model size, energy-accounting tables, and stability/ablation results do not test the listed scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits loss-versus-parameter power laws (L(N)=aN^b+c) for a new setting, 1-bit quantization-aware BitNet, alongside an FP16 Transformer baseline. It also tests a small-to-large fit extrapolation and downstream accuracy across scale. The method matches the originals, but the subject is a new architecture and training regime, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude BitNet follows a scaling law similar to full-precision Transformers and is competitive in perplexity and downstream accuracy with much lower memory and energy. They add that the gap to FP16 narrows with size and that BitNet is better at fixed inference energy. Accuracy of the small-to-large prediction is asserted without numbers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameter-count sweeps, loss curves, and power-law fitting, but applies them to a 1-bit quantization-aware Transformer (and an FP16 baseline), rather than reproducing the original studies' full setup. It does not test token scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

fits_no_version.finding: BitNet reaches lower loss than FP16 at a fixed estimated inference energy (an 'inference-optimal scaling law').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: 1-bit LMs give better loss per unit of inference energy than FP16 LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss gap between BitNet and FP16 shrinks as model size grows, implying different fitted scaling parameters for 1-bit weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight precision changes the scaling-curve parameters, with the precision penalty shrinking with scale.

record.problems: Scaling losses and downstream values are presented in figures without tabulated values or uncertainty estimates. The extrapolation is described as high accuracy but no numerical prediction errors are reported. The scaling experiment uses one stated English-language corpus setup and does not test token-count or training-compute scaling.
record.rows_left_out: Section 4, Table 3 reports post-training quantization comparisons at a single model size, not scaling results. Section 3.4, Figure 5 concerns training stability; Section 5, Table 4 concerns ablations. Table 1 and Section 2.3 report estimated arithmetic energy, not loss scaling.

untested.parts: Loss scaling in tokens or training compute. Parameter scaling is tested only at one fixed token budget (~10.5B), where data may bottleneck the largest models.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude (the tested span is under 5x). No extrapolation test for the FP16 baseline.
Entire version: no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Entire version: shape varies with size (Table 5) but is never isolated.
A quantitative fit of downstream accuracy against scale or loss. The authors themselves call capability harder to predict.
Entire version: no comparison of fitting methods, schedules or parameter-counting choices.

missing.what: Statement that the BitNet–FP16 loss gap narrows with model size; no row records it.
Zero- and few-shot accuracy across 1.3B–6.7B for BitNet and post-training-quantization baselines. rows_left_out cites only the single-size Table 3, not this scale series.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T3 because the main subject is a 1-bit quantization-aware architecture. All scaling evidence is figure-only, with no exponents, uncertainties or prediction errors. Figure 1 plots the fit out to 100B, but that is extrapolation, not data. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss against parameter count at fixed training tokens; does not test loss scaling against token count or training compute.
Tests extrapolation only for BitNet from 125M–6.7B to 13B and 30B; does not report an equivalent extrapolation test for FP16 Transformers.
No fixed training-compute-budget sweep over parameter and token allocations or measured compute-optimal split.
No comparison isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling experiment.
Reports downstream-task performance across scale, but does not test a quantitative relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, schedules, or datasets to test sensitivity of exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

source_check.reason: The power-law label is supported by Section 3.2 and Figure 3, but the token-total condition needs correction to fixed training tokens, total unspecified. Table 6 lists 40K updates and 256K tokens per sample, not per batch; deriving approximately 10.5B requires an unstated interpretation. Non-bottleneck conditions are not established.

relationships.reason: The authors state the fit predicted 13B and 30B loss with high accuracy (r3). The span is under one order of magnitude and no error values are given.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported accurate loss predictions for 13B and 30B models, less than one order of magnitude beyond the largest fitting model.
